title: Canonical Entity Modelling: Schema Evolution, SCD Type, and Delta Mutation Path
purpose: Make three recurring silver-modelling decisions explicit and show the mechanics behind each: whether an incoming schema change can merge automatically or is frozen by a foreign key constraint, whether a table needs SCD Type 2 history or a plain Type 1 overwrite, and whether the SCD write itself should use classic copy-on-write MERGE or deletion vectors — ending at the V-Order/OPTIMIZE physical-layout step every path still needs.
accessibleSummary: A decision and internals diagram covering three silver-layer modelling decisions. First, a schema-evolution question: an incoming bronze column change is additive and merges automatically via Delta mergeSchema, unless a foreign key constraint exists on the target table, which freezes all further schema evolution until removed. Second, a historization question: does any consumer need to reconstruct a row's state as of a past date; a yes routes to SCD Type 2 with an internals cutaway showing the close-old/open-new MERGE mechanics and a warning about non-deterministic latest-row ordering, while a no routes to SCD Type 1 in-place overwrite. Third, a Delta mutation-path question for the SCD Type 2 write itself: whether to use classic copy-on-write MERGE or enable deletion vectors, shown as an internals cutaway of the merge-on-read soft-delete-plus-small-file mechanism with its measured before/after-OPTIMIZE performance trade-off and Delta protocol version increase. A closing node shows the V-Order and OPTIMIZE physical-layout decision that every path still converges on, with its measured write-time cost.
longDescription: This is a decision and internals diagram, distinct from the bronze-to-silver pipeline flow: it goes one level deeper into three modelling choices a team makes while building the canonical entity itself, and shows the mechanism behind each rather than just naming it. Decision 1 asks whether an incoming bronze schema change is additive. Delta Lake's mergeSchema option lets new columns flow into the silver merge target automatically, but a documented trap sits right next to it: adding a foreign key constraint between endpoint tables freezes all further schema evolution on those tables, so a later, perfectly ordinary new-column change silently stops syncing — a symptom that looks like a stalled pipeline, not an error. Decision 2 asks the historization question: does any consumer genuinely need to reconstruct a row's state as of a past date? A yes routes to SCD Type 2, shown here with an internals cutaway of the actual MERGE mechanics — close the existing current row, open a new one — plus a dependency the diagram calls out explicitly with its own warning node: the merge requires a deterministic ordering key, and resolving 'latest row' by arrival or ingestion time instead of source commit time can silently produce a different history on every retry. A no routes to the simpler SCD Type 1 in-place overwrite, with Delta's own time travel remaining as an unmodelled (and time-bounded) recovery safety net. Decision 3 is new depth this diagram adds beyond the architecture diagram: for the SCD Type 2 write itself, should the underlying Delta mutation use classic copy-on-write MERGE, or deletion vectors? The internals cutaway shows deletion vectors' actual soft-delete mechanism — a small .bin marker file records which rows changed, and only a small new file carries the updated values, avoiding a full-file rewrite — with the benchmarked trade-off made explicit: roughly 3x less storage and 1.5x fewer files before OPTIMIZE runs, but reads measurably slow down (1.5x to 2.3x in the sourced benchmark) if OPTIMIZE never runs and markers accumulate, and enabling the feature permanently raises the table's Delta protocol version, which can lock out older readers. All three decisions converge on one shared step: V-Order and OPTIMIZE. None of Type 1, Type 2, copy-on-write, or deletion vectors eliminate the need for periodic compaction, and toggling the V-Order table property alone only changes future writes — existing files keep their old layout until a physical OPTIMIZE rewrite touches them.

nodes.label: New / changed bronze column arrives
nodes.summary: The schema-evolution root question: is this incoming change additive, or does it require review?
nodes.detail: Before a bronze schema change reaches the silver merge target, classify it: is it purely additive (a new column) or potentially breaking (a type narrowing, rename, or removal)? The answer determines whether Delta's mergeSchema can apply it automatically or whether it needs explicit review — and either way, it is worth checking whether a foreign key constraint on the target table is currently freezing evolution entirely.
nodes.whyItMatters: Treating every incoming schema change the same way is the two-sided failure mode this decision exists to prevent: auto-applying a breaking change corrupts downstream consumers expecting the old shape, while manually gatekeeping every additive change creates unnecessary process friction for the common, safe case.

inputs: An incoming bronze batch whose schema differs from the current silver table's schema
processing: Diff the incoming schema against the current silver table schema
Classify each difference as additive (new column) or breaking (type change, removal, rename)
Route additive changes toward automatic mergeSchema application
Route breaking changes toward explicit review
outputs: A classified schema change ready for either automatic merge or manual review
drill.example: A source system adds a loyalty_tier column with no other changes — a clean additive case that routes straight to mergeSchema.
controls: The additive-vs-breaking classification rule itself, since Delta's mergeSchema does not distinguish intent, only column presence
failureModes: Treating a type-narrowing change (e.g. decimal(18,2) to decimal(10,2)) as if it were purely additive and letting it merge automatically

nodes.label: mergeSchema · additive
nodes.summary: Delta's mergeSchema option applies additive schema changes to the silver merge target automatically.
nodes.detail: Delta Lake's mergeSchema option, set on a MERGE or write operation, lets new columns from the incoming batch flow into the target table's schema without a separate DDL step. This is a genuine Delta Lake platform capability, not something Fabric adds on top. A related, sourced platform behaviour on the same write path: under Spark's newer DataFrameWriterV2 API, calling replace() or createOrReplace() automatically overwrites a Delta table's schema and partitioning as a consequence of the method choice itself, without needing the separate overwriteSchema=true option that the older writer API requires for the same effect — a reminder that schema-evolution behaviour depends on which write API and method is used, not just the mergeSchema flag.
nodes.whyItMatters: Without mergeSchema, every new bronze column would require a manual ALTER TABLE before the next merge could succeed, turning a routine source change into a blocking incident; mergeSchema keeps genuinely additive evolution low-friction — but the DataFrameWriterV2 behaviour shows schema-overwrite semantics can also be triggered implicitly by method choice, not only by an explicit flag.

evidence.note: Calling replace() or createOrReplace() under DataFrameWriterV2 automatically overwrites a Delta table's schema and partitioning as a consequence of the method choice itself, without requiring the overwriteSchema=true option that V1 needs for the same effect.

inputs: An incoming batch classified as an additive schema change
processing: Set .option("mergeSchema", "true") on the MERGE or write operation
Delta appends the new column(s) to the target table's schema definition
Existing rows backfill the new column as null
outputs: An updated silver table schema with the new column present, no manual DDL required
drill.example: A loyalty_tier column newly present in the bronze batch flows into silver_customers via mergeSchema=true; existing rows show loyalty_tier=null until their next update.
controls: Whether mergeSchema is enabled per-operation or left off by default, forcing explicit review of every change
failureModes: Leaving mergeSchema on unconditionally and letting an unintended column (e.g. a debug field) flow into the canonical silver schema

nodes.label: Trap: FK constraint freezes evolution
nodes.summary: Adding a foreign key constraint between endpoint tables silently freezes further schema evolution on those tables.
nodes.detail: A documented, specific trap: once a foreign key constraint is added between endpoint tables, further schema changes on those tables — including ordinary additive changes like new columns — stop syncing until the constraint is addressed. The failure is silent: there is no error, only a sync that has quietly stopped keeping pace with the source schema.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the single most likely reason a team's mergeSchema-based additive-evolution pattern appears to 'stop working' for no visible reason; without knowing this trap exists, the natural diagnosis is a Spark or platform bug rather than a constraint someone added months earlier.

evidence.note: Adding a foreign key constraint between endpoint tables freezes further schema changes for those tables, so later Delta schema evolution (such as new columns) stops syncing until the constraint is addressed.

inputs: A silver or mirrored endpoint table that has a foreign key constraint defined against another table
processing: A subsequent bronze schema change (e.g. a new column) arrives
The FK constraint on the target table blocks the schema sync from applying it
No error surfaces — the sync simply stops reflecting new schema changes
outputs: A silver table whose schema has silently diverged from what mergeSchema alone would have produced
drill.example: A team adds a foreign key between silver_orders and silver_customers for referential documentation. Two months later, a new discount_code column added to bronze never appears in silver_orders — the team spends a day debugging Spark before finding the FK constraint is the cause.
controls: Auditing existing foreign key constraints on tables that need to keep evolving
Removing or reworking the constraint before relying on continued additive schema evolution
failureModes: Diagnosing the resulting stalled sync as a platform bug or a mergeSchema misconfiguration instead of checking for an FK constraint
Adding FK constraints for documentation purposes without realizing the schema-evolution cost

nodes.label: Any "as of" question?
nodes.summary: The historization root question: does any consumer need to reconstruct a row's state as of a past date?
nodes.detail: Ask whether any consumer genuinely needs to answer a point-in-time question — a price as it stood at time of sale, an address as it was when a contract was signed. If nobody does, SCD Type 2 is complexity with no customer, and a simpler Type 1 overwrite is the right call.
nodes.whyItMatters: SCD Type 2 changes the grain of the table, the shape of every downstream join, and the cost of every query against it. Adopting it speculatively imposes that cost permanently on a requirement that may never arrive.

inputs: The set of questions consumers actually ask of this entity
Regulatory or reconciliation requirements for point-in-time reconstruction
processing: List the questions asked of this entity by downstream consumers
Mark which ones require a past state rather than the current state
If none do, route to Type 1; otherwise route to Type 2
outputs: A yes/no routing to SCD Type 2 history or SCD Type 1 overwrite
drill.example: A product dimension is asked only 'what is this product called now', never 'what was it called when that order shipped' — so it routes to Type 1.
controls: Require a named 'as of' question before adopting Type 2, rather than applying it by convention
failureModes: Applying Type 2 to every dimension by habit and paying the join cost forever
Discovering the history requirement after the fact, with no way to reconstruct what an overwrite already destroyed

nodes.label: SCD Type 2 — MERGE internals
nodes.summary: The actual MERGE mechanics: close the existing current row, open a new current row.
nodes.detail: Under SCD Type 2, a tracked-attribute change closes the current version of the row (setting is_current=false and an effective-to date) and inserts a new version (is_current=true, effective-from the batch time), so the table holds every state the entity has ever been in with validity ranges. This is a modelling pattern implemented on top of Delta MERGE, not a Fabric-provided feature — and it depends on a deterministic ordering key, which is exactly where the adjacent warning node applies.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the only structure that answers 'as of' questions correctly. It is also the structure most often implemented with a subtly non-deterministic ordering, which corrupts history quietly rather than failing loudly.

inputs: Change records with a business key
A deterministic ordering column — source commit time or a monotonic sequence
The set of attributes whose change should trigger a new version
processing: Order changes deterministically by the ordering key, never by arrival order
In the MERGE WHEN MATCHED clause, close the current row by setting is_current=false and effective_to=batch_ts
In the WHEN NOT MATCHED clause, insert the new version with is_current=true and effective_from=batch_ts
Merge idempotently so a replayed batch does not create duplicate versions
outputs: A versioned Delta table with validity ranges per row
The ability to reconstruct any entity's state as of any past date
drill.example: A customer's address change is applied by source commit time; the previous row's validity is closed and a new row opened, so an order from last year still joins to the address that was current then.
controls: A deterministic ordering key, enforced and tested
An idempotent merge key so retries are safe
Which attributes are tracked for history versus overwritten in place
failureModes: Applying changes in arrival order rather than event order, producing a plausible but wrong history — see the adjacent warning node
A non-idempotent merge that duplicates versions when a batch is replayed

nodes.label: SCD Type 1 — overwrite
nodes.summary: No point-in-time requirement, so update in place and skip the versioning cost.
nodes.detail: Where only the current state is ever asked for, the MERGE updates the matching row in place with no history row inserted. Delta still supplies ACID guarantees and time travel over the underlying Parquet files, so a limited amount of history remains recoverable without modelling it explicitly as a business concept.
nodes.whyItMatters: It keeps the table at its natural grain and its joins simple. Delta's time travel means choosing this does not leave you with literally no recourse if a past state is needed for recovery — though that recourse is time-bounded and not a substitute for modelled history.

evidence.note: All managed lakehouse tables use Delta, which supplies ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel over the underlying Parquet files.

inputs: A business key to match on
processing: MERGE on the business key, updating matched rows in place
Insert unmatched (new) rows with no versioning logic
outputs: A current-state table at its natural grain
Delta time travel available for recovery, though not modelled as business history
drill.example: A product reference table is merged on product key each night; only the current name and category are kept, and Delta time travel covers accidental-overwrite recovery.
controls: Do not lean on Delta time travel as if it were business history — retention is bounded
failureModes: Treating time travel as an SCD Type 2 substitute and discovering the retention window has passed when a real point-in-time need arrives

nodes.label: Trap: unstable "latest row" key
nodes.summary: Resolving the latest row per key without a deterministic ordering column corrupts history — differently on every retry.
nodes.detail: The classic silver bug: deduplicating to the 'latest' row per business key using arrival order, file order, or an unstable timestamp. It usually looks correct, because most of the time the orders coincide. On a retry, a late-arriving file, or a reshuffled partition, it silently picks a different winner — and an SCD Type 2 table built on it records a history that never happened.
nodes.whyItMatters: The failure is non-deterministic, so it does not reproduce on demand and it does not fail loudly. It just quietly writes a different history each time the job runs, and the corruption is typically only discovered during an audit or a customer dispute, long after the offending batch has aged out of retention.

inputs: Change records with more than one row per business key in a batch
The column currently being used to decide which one wins
processing: Identify a genuinely deterministic ordering key — source commit time, a monotonic sequence, or an LSN
Break ties explicitly, so two rows with the same timestamp still resolve identically every run
Make the merge idempotent so a replay reproduces the same result exactly
outputs: Deduplication that produces the same winner on every run
An SCD Type 2 history that is reproducible rather than incidental
drill.example: A Spark retry re-reads the same micro-batch after a transient executor failure; because the dedup stage ordered by ingestion timestamp (which shifts on retry) rather than the source system's commit sequence, the retried run picks a different row as 'latest' than the original attempt, silently rewriting which address is marked current for that customer.
controls: A deterministic ordering key plus an explicit tiebreak, tested with a deliberately reordered replay
failureModes: Using ingestion or file-arrival time as if it were event time
Assuming a same-second tie will not happen, so leaving the tiebreak undefined

nodes.label: Copy-on-write MERGE, or deletion vectors?
nodes.summary: The Delta mutation-path root question for the SCD Type 2 write itself.
nodes.detail: The SCD Type 2 merge can execute as classic copy-on-write MERGE, which rewrites entire Parquet files that contain a changed row, or with deletion vectors enabled, which shifts the mutation to merge-on-read. Frequent row-level UPDATE/MERGE traffic on this table changes which path is actually cheaper — this is a genuine engineering trade-off, not a default either engine picks for you.
nodes.whyItMatters: Choosing between these two mutation paths is invisible in the modelling logic itself (the MERGE statement looks the same either way) but has a real, measurable effect on write cost, storage, and read performance depending on mutation frequency and whether OPTIMIZE actually runs afterward.

inputs: The SCD Type 2 table's expected row-level UPDATE/MERGE frequency
Whether a periodic OPTIMIZE job can realistically be scheduled and maintained for this table
processing: Estimate the proportion of writes that are row-level mutations versus append-only inserts
Weigh storage/write-time savings from deletion vectors against the read-side risk if OPTIMIZE lapses
Confirm downstream readers support the resulting Delta protocol version before enabling deletion vectors
outputs: A chosen mutation path for the SCD merge, plus (if deletion vectors) a committed OPTIMIZE cadence
drill.example: A frequently-updated customer table with daily GDPR delete requests evaluates deletion vectors against its OPTIMIZE-scheduling capacity before enabling them.
controls: Whether deletion vectors are enabled at the table level
The OPTIMIZE cadence committed to alongside that choice
failureModes: Enabling deletion vectors for the write-time win without committing to the OPTIMIZE cadence it depends on

nodes.label: Deletion vectors — merge-on-read
nodes.summary: UPDATE soft-deletes the old row via a small marker file instead of rewriting the whole file.
nodes.detail: Deletion vectors shift Delta Lake mutations from copy-on-write to merge-on-read. For an UPDATE, the old version of a changed row is soft-deleted in its existing Parquet file via a new small binary (.bin) marker record, and only the updated row values are written to a new, smaller Parquet file — avoiding a full rewrite of the source file. Before any OPTIMIZE runs, this produced roughly 3x less storage and about 1.5x fewer files than the copy-on-write baseline in a sourced benchmark. But if deletion vectors accumulate without periodic OPTIMIZE, read performance degrades: a heavy non-append-change scenario ran 2.3x slower, and a MERGE-only scenario ran 1.5x slower, than the copy-on-write baseline in the same benchmark. Enabling the feature also permanently raises the table's minReaderVersion to 3 and minWriterVersion to 7 (Delta protocol 2.3+), which older readers cannot open.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is a genuine performance win that inverts into a genuine performance regression if the OPTIMIZE half of the pattern is skipped — and because writes stay fast the whole time, nothing in the write path signals the read-side cost building up.

evidence.note: Deletion vectors shift Delta Lake mutations from copy-on-write to merge-on-read: rather than rewriting entire Parquet files for any changed record, the system records the positions of affected rows in a small binary file and filters those rows out at query time.

For UPDATE operations, deletion vectors soft-delete the old version of changed rows in their existing Parquet file via a new .bin record, then write only the updated row values to a new, smaller Parquet file — avoiding a full rewrite of the source file.

Before running OPTIMIZE, deletion vectors produced about 3x less storage (2,351 MB versus 7,705 MB) and roughly 1.5x fewer files than the copy-on-write baseline in the author's benchmark, because soft-deletes avoid rewriting large unchanged files.

If deletion vectors accumulate without periodic OPTIMIZE, read performance degrades: the author's benchmark showed a scenario with 53% non-append changes and no compaction running 2.3x slower, and a MERGE-only scenario with 5M new records running 1.5x slower than the copy-on-write baseline.

Enabling deletion vectors permanently raises a table's minReaderVersion to 3 and minWriterVersion to 7, requiring Delta reader/writer protocol version 2.3 or later; downstream consumers that do not support these versions will be unable to read the table.

inputs: A table with frequent row-level UPDATE, DELETE, or MERGE traffic considering deletion vectors
processing: Enable deletion vectors on the table (raises minReaderVersion/minWriterVersion)
Route mutations through the merge-on-read path: soft-delete via marker file, write only changed values
Schedule periodic OPTIMIZE to compact accumulated markers before read performance degrades
outputs: Faster individual mutations and lower storage before compaction, at the cost of a stricter Delta protocol version and an ongoing dependency on OPTIMIZE
drill.example: A customer table processing daily GDPR delete requests enables deletion vectors and gets roughly 3x smaller storage and 1.5x fewer files before its first OPTIMIZE; a weekly OPTIMIZE then keeps read performance from degrading as markers accumulate.
controls: Confirm downstream consumers support Delta protocol 2.3+ before enabling
Schedule OPTIMIZE on a cadence matched to mutation volume
failureModes: Enabling deletion vectors and never scheduling OPTIMIZE, letting read performance silently degrade 1.5x–2.3x as markers accumulate
A downstream reader or older tool incompatible with Delta protocol 2.3+ losing read access to the table

metrics.label: Storage before OPTIMIZE vs copy-on-write
metrics.value: ~3x smaller (2,351 MB vs 7,705 MB in benchmark)

metrics.label: Read slowdown if OPTIMIZE never runs

nodes.label: V-Order + OPTIMIZE — the shared physical-layout step
nodes.summary: Every modelling path above still needs periodic OPTIMIZE; the V-Order table property alone only affects future writes.
nodes.detail: Regardless of which schema-evolution, SCD type, or mutation-path decision was made, the resulting table still needs periodic OPTIMIZE (compaction), and V-Order — a write-time Parquet reorganization that speeds downstream reads — can be applied during that same compaction pass. Microsoft states the typical cost as writes taking roughly 15% longer on average. Critically, toggling the V-Order table property changes only future writes: files already on disk keep the layout they were written with, so applying V-Order to existing data requires the physical rewrite that OPTIMIZE performs.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the convergence point that makes the three decisions above genuinely independent of physical layout: none of Type 1, Type 2, copy-on-write, or deletion vectors substitute for compaction, and teams that enable V-Order and see no improvement have usually just skipped the OPTIMIZE step that actually applies it.

evidence.note: Toggling the V-Order table property only affects future writes; files already on disk keep the layout they were written with, so applying or removing V-Order on existing data requires a physical rewrite via table compaction (OPTIMIZE).
Microsoft states the typical V-Order tradeoff as writes taking roughly 15% longer on average, in exchange for reads that can improve significantly depending on the workload.

V-Order is disabled by default in all newly created Fabric workspaces (spark.sql.parquet.vorder.default=false), a deliberate default that favors write-heavy ingestion and transformation pipelines over read optimization.

inputs: A silver table produced by any of the three decision paths above, accumulating small files from repeated writes
processing: Classify the table as read-heavy or write-heavy
For read-heavy tables, enable V-Order (session, table property, or per-write) and run OPTIMIZE to apply it to existing files
For write-heavy tables, leave V-Order off, matching the platform default
outputs: A compacted, appropriately V-Ordered silver table regardless of which schema-evolution, SCD, or mutation-path decision produced it
drill.example: A gold-facing silver_customers table built with SCD Type 2 and deletion vectors gets V-Order enabled and a weekly OPTIMIZE once dashboards start querying it heavily; a write-heavy staging table built with SCD Type 1 stays on the workspace default of V-Order off.
controls: Whether V-Order is enabled for this table's compaction pass
failureModes: Enabling the V-Order property and never running OPTIMIZE, then concluding V-Order does not work
Enabling V-Order on a write-dominated table and paying the ~15% write cost for a read benefit nobody uses

walkthrough.title: 1. Classify the incoming schema change
walkthrough.explanation: Before an incoming bronze column change reaches the silver merge target, decide whether it is purely additive or potentially breaking.

walkthrough.title: 2a. Additive changes flow in via mergeSchema
walkthrough.explanation: Delta's mergeSchema option on the MERGE/write operation lets new columns flow into the silver schema automatically, no manual DDL required.

walkthrough.title: 2b. Warning: a foreign key constraint can freeze this silently
walkthrough.explanation: Adding an FK constraint between endpoint tables freezes further schema evolution on those tables — with no visible error, only a stalled sync.

walkthrough.title: 3. Ask the historization question
walkthrough.explanation: Does any consumer genuinely need to reconstruct a row's state as of a past date? SCD Type 2 is only justified by a real point-in-time requirement.

walkthrough.title: 4a. If yes, see the actual MERGE mechanics
walkthrough.explanation: SCD Type 2 closes the existing current row and opens a new one — mechanics that depend entirely on a deterministic ordering key.

walkthrough.title: 4b. Warning: an unstable ordering key corrupts history
walkthrough.explanation: Resolving 'latest row' by arrival time instead of source commit time can silently produce a different SCD history on every retry — and it doesn't fail loudly.

walkthrough.title: 5. If no, overwrite in place
walkthrough.explanation: SCD Type 1 updates the matching row with no history kept; Delta time travel remains as a bounded, unmodelled recovery net.

walkthrough.title: 6. Choose the Delta mutation path for the write
walkthrough.explanation: Independent of SCD type, decide whether the underlying write should be classic copy-on-write MERGE or deletion vectors.

walkthrough.title: 7. See the deletion-vector soft-delete mechanism
walkthrough.explanation: A small marker file records changed rows instead of a full-file rewrite — a real storage and write-time win that inverts into a read-time cost if OPTIMIZE never runs.

walkthrough.title: 8. Every path converges on V-Order + OPTIMIZE
walkthrough.explanation: None of the schema-evolution, SCD-type, or mutation-path decisions substitute for periodic compaction, and the V-Order property only affects future writes until OPTIMIZE physically rewrites existing files.
